title: Composite Indexes for Multiple Equality Predicates
description: With only a single-column index the optimizer gives up and scans on two predicates; a composite index over both seeks precisely. Why it matters: multi-condition filters are the norm in real application queries -- this is a foundational skill for designing indexes that actually get used.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine a phone book that's only organized alphabetically by first name. If you're looking for someone named "John," you can jump straight to the "J" section — that part's easy. But if you also need that John to live on a specific street, the phone book gives you no help at all for the second condition; you still have to check every single "John" entry one at a time to see which ones happen to live on that street. This lesson is about that exact limitation, and about what happens when a query filters on two conditions but only has an index that helps with one of them.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** This lesson is about composite indexes — indexes built on more than one column together, in a specific, deliberate order — and about why a query filtering on two separate conditions (two equality predicates, like `WHERE Status = 'X' AND Region = 'Y'`) often can't be efficiently served by two separate single-column indexes, even though it seems like it should be able to combine them.

**Why this happens in real databases.** Multi-condition filters are the norm in real applications, not the exception — almost every meaningful search, report, or list screen filters on more than one thing at once ("active customers in this region," "orders with this status placed this month"). It's intuitive to assume that if you have an index on column A and a separate index on column B, SQL Server can somehow use both together to satisfy `WHERE A = ... AND B = ...` efficiently. In practice, that combination is often expensive or simply not chosen, because each index, individually, only narrows things down along its own single dimension — an index on `Status` alone can find "all rows with this status," but among those, it still has no fast way to further narrow down "which of these also matches this region," because region isn't part of that index's structure at all.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** A single-column index is sorted (or structured) purely by the values in that one column. Using the index on `Status` to satisfy `WHERE Status = 'X'` gets you, very efficiently, exactly the set of rows with that status — but within that result, the rows are not organized in any way by `Region` at all, so checking `AND Region = 'Y'` against each of them means examining every single row in that status-matching set individually, one at a time, to see whether it also happens to satisfy the region condition. If a lot of rows share that status, that's still a lot of individual checking, even though the initial narrowing worked. Given only two single-column indexes like this, the optimizer often decides it's not worth trying to cleverly intersect them (that intersection strategy exists but has its own overhead and doesn't always pay off) and instead just picks whichever single column narrows things down the most, then filters the rest via that same slow one-at-a-time checking, or gives up and scans the whole table if neither index looks selective enough on its own.

A composite index changes this completely by physically storing rows sorted first by the first column, and then, within each group of matching first-column values, sorted by the second column. So an index built as `(Status, Region)` stores all the rows with a given status grouped together, and within that group, further sorted by region. Now a query filtering on both `Status = 'X' AND Region = 'Y'` can seek directly to exactly the narrow slice of the index where both conditions are already true simultaneously — no separate second pass, no row-by-row checking of a partially-narrowed set, just one direct seek straight to the precise matching rows, because the index itself already groups the data by both conditions together, not just one.

**Why this matters in production.** This pattern — a report or search screen slowing down badly the moment a second filter condition is added, even though both columns individually have "an index" — is one of the most common real-world indexing mistakes, precisely because it's counterintuitive that two single-column indexes don't automatically combine as efficiently as one well-designed composite index covering both columns together. The fix in this lesson is exactly that: replacing (or adding to) the single-column indexes with one composite index over both filtered columns, in an order that matches how the query actually filters, which turns two conditions worth of filtering into a single precise index seek rather than a seek-plus-scan-the-rest.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below filters on two separate equality conditions with only single-column indexes available, and shows you the plan falling back to a scan or an inefficient partial-narrowing strategy. After replacing the single-column indexes with one composite index covering both filtered columns, re-run the same query and watch the plan collapse to a single, precise Index Seek — a direct before-and-after look at how much more targeted a seek becomes once the index itself already groups the data by both conditions together, rather than just one.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** Composite index column order matters beyond just "which columns are included" — as a rule of thumb, equality predicates (`= value`) should generally come before range predicates (`BETWEEN`, `>`, `<`) in a composite index's column order, because once the index hits a range condition, it can no longer use any columns listed after it to narrow the seek further; everything past that point in the index falls back to being checked row by row within the matching range. This lesson's two equality predicates are the simplest case, but the same equality-before-range principle extends directly to composite indexes that combine equality filters with a date range or numeric range, which is one of the single most common index-design decisions in real schemas.

It's also worth remembering that column order in a composite index is not interchangeable — an index on `(Status, Region)` helps a query filtering on `Status` alone, or on both columns together, but does little to help a query filtering on `Region` alone, since the index isn't sorted by region except within each individual status group.

## Scenario
A support screen looks up one customer's open orders: `WHERE Status = 'Open' AND CustomerId = 42`. There is an index on `Status`, yet the query is slow.

## Why it's slow
The only index, `IX_Orders_Status`, keys on **Status alone**. `Status = 'Open'` matches **~66,000 rows** (a third of the table). SQL Server must then test `CustomerId = 42` as a **residual predicate** on every one of those rows — and because the index doesn't cover `CustomerId`, each candidate needs a lookup. Faced with that cost the optimizer typically abandons the index and just does a **Clustered Index Scan** of all 200k rows.

## The concept
An index on a **single** column of a multi-predicate filter only narrows *one* dimension. A **composite index keyed on both equality columns** — `(Status, CustomerId)` — lets the engine seek directly to the tiny intersection (~13 rows). Add `INCLUDE (OrderDate, Total)` so the index **covers** the SELECT and no lookup is needed.

## What to look for
- Bad: a **Clustered Index Scan** (or a Status seek reading tens of thousands of rows).
- Good: a single **Index Seek** on `(Status, CustomerId)`, a handful of logical reads.

> Contrast with the composite-**key-order** lesson (i-04): there the concern is which column leads for a *range*. Here both predicates are **equality**, so both belong in the key.
hints: IX_Orders_Status keys on Status only. Status = 'Open' matches ~66k rows, so CustomerId is just a filter applied afterward.
You need an index that can seek on BOTH equality columns at once — put them both in the key.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Status_Cust ON Orders(Status, CustomerId) INCLUDE (OrderDate, Total); then re-run the query.
